title: What the checker actually checks
dek: What a post-training grader audit, an adaptive-learning rubric, and a formal proof reveal about the limits of automated checks.

sections.title: An aggregate can agree for the wrong reason
paragraphs: In an early Countdown training run, the original grader and its corrected replacement both awarded exactly one successful rollout out of 256. If I had compared only the batch accuracy, the repair would have looked irrelevant. The two graders had rewarded different rollouts.

The model was not stopped at its first closing answer tag. It continued writing, often inventing another user question and answering that instead. The original parser selected the last answer block. A later answer could accidentally solve the actual task even when the first answer did not; a later invented task could also obscure a correct first answer.

Re-scoring the retained batch found 166 extraction disagreements, one false positive and one false negative. Nearly 86% of the generated text came after the first answer. The arithmetic checker was evaluating expressions, but the surrounding system had not reliably identified which expression was the submitted answer.

sections.title: The specification includes the boundary
paragraphs: The repair had two parts: stop generation at the closing answer tag, and grade the first answer after the reasoning section. Regression checks preserve both requirements. Fixing the parser alone would leave unnecessary continuation in the rollout; changing generation alone would leave a fragile scorer for older or malformed outputs.

This example is a grading vulnerability with observed consequences for reward assignment. It is not evidence that reinforcement learning taught the model to exploit the bug. Only one batch remains from the stopped first run, and a convincing claim of learned exploitation would require evidence about how the relevant behavior changed under optimization.

That distinction matters because an explanation can outrun its data. “The grader can reward the wrong answer” and “the agent learned to game the grader” motivate related investigations, but they are different empirical claims.

sections.title: A repaired score still needs interpretation
paragraphs: After the repair, Countdown per-attempt accuracy rose from 1.3% at the base model to 55.7% at the final checkpoint. The evaluation used the same 256 puzzles and 32 samples per puzzle. Yet pass@32 reached 55.1% by step 50 and ended at 56.2%.

The later training mostly made successful answers more likely on a limited set of puzzles. A single rising accuracy curve would have hidden that structure. Matching the sampling budget and inspecting puzzle-level outcomes makes the interpretation more precise. The puzzles were excluded from training updates, but monitored during development; they were not an untouched final confirmation set.

A checker can tell us whether an answer passes its rule. Understanding what improved requires another layer of measurement: coverage, reliability, sampling, task difficulty and the ways the evaluation itself informed development.

sections.title: The same problem appears in a learning product
paragraphs: Cognanimus checks numeric and structured answers locally and uses explicit rubrics for written work. That separation limits what a language-model judgment can control, but it does not make the rubric automatically correct.

One grading investigation found a hidden requirement: a response explained what the question asked, while the rubric also demanded additional information. The system was enforcing a criterion that the learner had not been given. The repair changed the public criteria and kept the historical submission and correction record.

Another case exposed an ambiguous partial-credit boundary. The expected score remained fixed, the rubric was clarified, and an opposite-side boundary case was added so the fix would not simply suppress valid partial credit. Passing examples become more informative when the neighboring failure cases are explicit.

sections.title: Formal verification sharpens the promise
paragraphs: The BusyCoq contributions use a stronger acceptance mechanism: exact machine statements checked by Rocq/Coq. Search can propose an invariant or an accelerated execution batch, while a separate checker decides whether the proof follows from the framework.

Even here, the claim must match the theorem. One accepted submission proves that a machine halts. The approximately 1.77 × 10^44 step count is computed separately; that number is not proved by the halting theorem. The assumption report is also part of the result, not an implementation footnote.

Across these projects, my working rule is to keep four things together: the intended task, the exact accepted object, the evidence for accepting it and the claim the result supports. Mechanical checks are valuable precisely because their scope can be inspected. Their usefulness increases when the surrounding experiment and explanation respect that scope.

title: When steering changes nothing
dek: Activation steering on Qwen3-32B changed the model’s activations without changing its stopping behavior in the tested conditions.

sections.title: A useful representation is only the first step
paragraphs: The research question begins with an appealing possibility: internal representations associated with curiosity or satisfaction might help explain whether a language model seeks information or stops. To study that possibility, I need to separate three claims. The model may represent descriptions of a state; that representation may influence its behavior; the behavior may bear on experience. Evidence for one does not automatically establish the next.

The completed studies use Qwen3-32B with unchanged weights. The first constructed activation contrasts from two separately authored narrative corpora. Corpus A supplied the fitted directions and layer selection. Corpus B tested transfer without selecting a new direction or threshold. The frozen earliest-layer tie rule chose layer 15.

sections.title: Transfer did not establish specificity
paragraphs: Both the curiosity and satisfaction candidates correctly ordered all twelve target pairs in corpus B. But the curiosity direction also separated general motivation and interest in novelty. Satisfaction’s fixed threshold correctly classified only fourteen of twenty-four B descriptions. A direction can preserve relative ordering while failing as a calibrated classifier in a new context.

These were descriptions of narrators, not demonstrations of the model’s own motivation. The next step was therefore a task with an independent oracle: finite worlds where the hidden answer, supplied facts and information value of each report were mechanically known. The model could request another report or stop.

The behavioral pattern was simple: seek informative reports while unresolved and stop after decisive evidence. The two-family assay nevertheless failed a comprehension gate. In one family, the model treated possible values in a candidate table as though those observations had already been supplied. The predicted natural satisfaction increase also failed. Those failures constrained the next experiment rather than disappearing from its introduction.

sections.title: Test the imposed direction on its own terms
paragraphs: The next screen was explicitly exploratory and restricted to the object family, which had passed the earlier diagnostics. Twenty-four worlds were crossed with four arms: untouched baseline, an installed zero-dose sham and two positive satisfaction-direction doses. Each arm contained 144 choices and 144 diagnostic responses.

The intervention applied the fixed direction at a record boundary during prefill and at subsequent active generated-token positions. Before examining outcomes, the plan fixed the candidate, site, sign, doses, prompts, scoring rules and advancement threshold. The primary +1.0 arm had to increase valid stopping after redundant evidence by at least twenty-five percentage points in each panel, with every readiness gate satisfied. The half-dose could not replace it.

All 1,152 generation records were retained. Every condition selected an informative report in all 96 unresolved choices and stopped in all 48 resolved choices. The primary stopping contrast was zero in both panels. Its response-validity gate also failed: one diagnostic produced an explanation ending in a boxed answer instead of the required single letter. The half-dose passed its diagnostics and still changed no choices.

sections.title: Check that nothing happened for the reason you think
paragraphs: A null outcome is difficult to interpret if the intervention might never have run. Here, the installed zero sham matched baseline tokens and full-vocabulary outputs exactly. Positive arms showed nonzero perturbations and the expected local projection change. Pre-intervention vectors matched across arms, hooks were cleaned up and all assignments were accounted for.

Median perturbations were approximately eleven and twenty-three percent of the native residual norm. That is evidence of local activation engagement. It is not evidence that the perturbation engaged satisfaction as a natural psychological variable. Prefill geometry was independently reconstructed; decode geometry was checked against scalar ledgers and the tested engine, without a second reconstruction from saved per-token residual vectors.

The distinction prevents an easy overclaim in either direction. Verified steering with unchanged behavior does not prove that satisfaction-like mechanisms are absent. It does show that this fixed candidate and schedule did not produce the proposed effect in these observed tasks.

sections.title: Preserve the boundary of the result
paragraphs: The study is small and developmental. Twenty of the twenty-four worlds had partial projected-table exposure in earlier work. Treatment arms were aligned with worker instances, despite model, arithmetic and pre-intervention matching checks. The object-only selection followed a failed broader assay. A bootstrap interval of zero to zero reflects identical observed choices; it is not population-wide equivalence.

The fixed screen ended without a positive result. The public snapshot includes all outcome rows, the readiness cells and the failed natural-resolution evidence. Its value is a narrower question answered carefully: this semantic candidate transferred between descriptions, yet neither the natural measurement nor the imposed intervention established the proposed motivational role.

A future experiment can investigate a different candidate or mechanism, provided that it is identified as new work. Keeping the completed negative result intact makes that next question easier to evaluate—and keeps an interesting hypothesis from turning into a conclusion by repetition.
